MO theory provides considerably more insight into the origin of the crystal field splitting, however, and a satisfactory ex­ planation for the trends observed in the spectrochemical series that could not be provided by the earlier theories. p or­ bitals; the crystal field splitting o is the energy difference between them. The ener­ gies of the nb orbitals are unaffected by bonding, but the energies of the d

p orbit­ als that lie above them are determined by the strength of the metal-ligand bonds. Recall from Section 6.5 that the energy of bonding MOs decreases with increasing bond strength while the energy of the corresponding antibonding MOs increases with increasing bond strength. The increase in crystal field splitting observed through the middle of the spectrochemical series correlates well with the strength of the metal-ligand s bonds, but MO theory cannot account for the order observed throughout the rest of the series without considering p bonding.

Let’s consider the effects of p bonding by first examining the nature of the bonds formed between a metal atom or ion and a single ligand. We then extend the treat­ ment to examine the effects of p bonding on the energy level structure and properties of octahedral complexes. Figure 8.29a shows a bonding and an antibonding MO constructed from a metal d orbital and a ligand p orbital oriented “side-by-side.” These MOs are typical for metals with few d electrons, such as Cr31, and for ligands with filled p orbitals that lie close to, but somewhat lower than, the energy of the metal d orbitals, for example, the 3p orbitals of Cl2. The empty 4p ligand orbitals are not considered because they lie too high in energy. The bonding p orbital is primarily ligand in character, because the ligand orbitals are lower in energy than the metal orbitals; the antibonding p* orbital is primarily metal in character for the same rea­ son. The bonding orbital is populated by charge donation from the filled ligand orbit­ als; we call this kind of bonding (L→M) p donation, by analogy to that just described for (L→M) s donation. Figure 8.29b illustrates the opposite situation in which the filled ligand orbitals lie at much lower energies than the metal orbitals and do not participate in bonding. There is an empty ligand p* orbital, however, that is suffi­ ciently close in energy and of the correct symmetry that it can overlap with the metal d orbital to form a bonding and an antibonding MO by overlapping the metal orbital “side-by-side,” as shown. The character of the bonding MO is largely determined by the character of the lower energy metal orbital, and it is filled by electrons transferred
